[[file:ObjectiveStressRates.png|thumb|300px|Predictions from three objective stress rates under shear]]
In [[continuum mechanics]], '''objective stress rates''' are time [[derivative]]s of [[stress (physics)|stress]] that do not depend on the [[frame of reference]].<ref name="Gurtin" /> Many [[constitutive equation]]s are designed in the form of a relation between a stress-rate and a [[finite strain theory|strain-rate]] (or the [[finite strain theory|rate of deformation]] tensor). The mechanical response of a material should not depend on the frame of reference. In other words, material constitutive equations should be [[material objectivity|frame-indifferent (objective)]]. If the [[stress measures|stress]] and strain measures are [[Continuum mechanics#Lagrangian description|material]] quantities then objectivity is automatically satisfied. However, if the quantities are [[Continuum mechanics#Eulerian description|spatial]], then the objectivity of the stress-rate is not guaranteed even if the strain-rate is objective.

There are numerous objective stress rates in continuum mechanics – all of which can be shown to be special forms of [[Lie derivative]]s. Some of the widely used objective stress rates are:
# the ''' Truesdell''' rate of the [[Cauchy stress tensor]],
# the ''' Green–Naghdi''' rate of the Cauchy stress, and
# the ''' Zaremba-Jaumann''' rate of the Cauchy stress.<ref>Zaremba, [https://ci.nii.ac.jp/naid/10011562502/ "Sur une forme perfectionée de la théorie de la relaxation"], ''Bull. Int. Acad. Sci. Cracovie'', 1903.</ref>

The adjacent figure shows the performance of various objective rates in a [[simple shear]] test where the material model is [[hypoelastic material|hypoelastic]] with constant [[elastic moduli]]. The ratio of the [[shear stress]] to the [[displacement field (mechanics)|displacement]] is plotted as a function of time. The same moduli are used with the three objective stress rates. Clearly there are spurious oscillations observed for the Zaremba-Jaumann stress rate.<ref>{{cite news|last=Dienes|first=J.|title=On the analysis of rotation and stress rate in deforming bodies.|year=1979|journal=Acta Mechanica|volume=32|page=217}}</ref>
This is not because one rate is better than another but because it is a misuse of material models to use the same constants with different objective rates.<ref>{{cite news|last=Brannon|first=R.M.|title=Caveats concerning conjugate stress and strain measures for frame indifferent anisotropic elasticity.|year=1998|journal=Acta Mechanica|volume=129|pages=107–116}}</ref> For this reason, a recent trend has been to avoid objective stress rates altogether where possible.{{Citation needed|date=March 2016}}

== Non-objectivity of the time derivative of Cauchy stress ==
Under rigid body rotations (<math>\boldsymbol{Q}</math>), the [[Cauchy stress tensor]] <math>\boldsymbol{\sigma}</math> [[Cauchy stress tensor#Transformation rule of the stress tensor|transform]]s as
<math display="block"> \boldsymbol{\sigma}_r = \boldsymbol{Q}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\boldsymbol{Q}^T ~;~~ \boldsymbol{Q}\cdot\boldsymbol{Q}^T = \boldsymbol{\mathit{1}}</math>
Since <math>\boldsymbol{\sigma}</math> is a spatial quantity and the transformation follows the rules of [[covariant transformation|tensor transformation]]s, <math>\boldsymbol{\sigma}</math> is objective.  However,
<math display="block">
  \cfrac{d}{dt}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}_r) = \dot{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_r = \dot{\boldsymbol{Q}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\boldsymbol{Q}^T +
    \boldsymbol{Q}\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\cdot\boldsymbol{Q}^T + \boldsymbol{Q}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol{Q}}^T \ne \boldsymbol{Q}\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\cdot\boldsymbol{Q}^T \,.
</math>
Therefore, the stress rate is ''' not objective''' unless the rate of rotation is zero, i.e. <math>\boldsymbol{Q}</math> is constant.

[[File:Undeformed and deformed material element.svg|300px|right|thumb|Figure 1. Undeformed and deformed material element, and an elemental cube cut out from the deformed element.]]
For a physical understanding of the above, consider the situation shown in Figure 1. In the figure the components of the Cauchy (or true) stress tensor are denoted by the symbols <math>S_{ij}</math>. This tensor, which describes the forces on a small material element imagined to be cut out from the material as currently deformed, is not objective at large deformations because it varies with rigid body rotations of the material. The material points must be characterized by their initial Lagrangian coordinates <math>X_i</math>. Consequently, it is necessary to introduce the so-called objective stress rate <math>\overset{\circ}{S}_{ij}</math>, or the corresponding increment <math>\Delta S_{ij} = \overset{\circ}{S}_{ij} \Delta t</math>. The objectivity is necessary for <math>\overset{\circ}{S}_{ij}</math> to be functionally related to the element deformation. It means that <math>\overset{\circ}{S}_{ij}</math> must be invariant with respect to coordinate transformations, particularly the rigid-body rotations, and must characterize the state of the same material element as it deforms.

The objective stress rate can be derived in two ways:
* by tensorial coordinate transformations,<ref name="HibMarRic70" /> which is the standard way in finite element textbooks<ref name="BelLiuMor00" />
* variationally, from strain energy density in the material expressed in terms of the strain tensor (which is objective by definition)<ref name="Baz71" /><ref name="BazCed91" />

While the former way is instructive and provides useful geometric insight, the latter way is mathematically shorter and has the additional advantage of automatically ensuring [[energy conservation]], i.e., guaranteeing that the second-order work of the stress increment tensor on the strain increment tensor be correct (work conjugacy requirement).

==Truesdell stress rate of the Cauchy stress==
The relation between the Cauchy stress and the 2nd P-K stress is called
the ''' Piola transformation'''. This transformation can be 
written in terms of the pull-back of <math>\boldsymbol{\sigma}</math> or the push-forward of <math>\boldsymbol{S}</math> as
<math display="block"> \boldsymbol{S} = J~\phi^{*}[\boldsymbol{\sigma}] ~;~~ \boldsymbol{\sigma} = J^{-1}~\phi_{*}[\boldsymbol{S}] </math>

The ''' Truesdell rate''' of the Cauchy stress is the Piola transformation of the material [[time derivative]] of the 2nd P-K stress. We thus define
<math display="block"> \overset{\circ}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} = J^{-1}~\phi_{*}[\dot{\boldsymbol{S}}] </math>

Expanded out, this means that

<math display="block">
  \overset{\circ}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} = J^{-1}~\boldsymbol{F}\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol{S}}\cdot\boldsymbol{F}^T
     = J^{-1}~\boldsymbol{F}\cdot
       \left[\cfrac{d}{dt}\left(J~\boldsymbol{F}^{-1}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\boldsymbol{F}^{-T}\right)\right]
       \cdot\boldsymbol{F}^T
     = J^{-1}~\mathcal{L}_\varphi[\boldsymbol{\tau}]
</math>
where the Kirchhoff stress <math>\boldsymbol{\tau} = J~\boldsymbol{\sigma}</math> and the ''' Lie derivative''' of 
the Kirchhoff stress is
<math display="block">
  \mathcal{L}_\varphi[\boldsymbol{\tau}] = \boldsymbol{F}\cdot
       \left[\cfrac{d}{dt}\left(\boldsymbol{F}^{-1}\cdot\boldsymbol{\tau}\cdot\boldsymbol{F}^{-T}\right)\right]
       \cdot\boldsymbol{F}^T ~.
</math>

This expression can be simplified to the well known expression for the Truesdell rate of the Cauchy stress
<!-- TODO: replace with equation boxes? -->
{| cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" style="margin:0em 0em 1em 0em; width:80%"
| colspan="2" style="width:80%; horizontal-align:right; vertical-align:top; border:1px solid Sienna; background-color:White;" |
<div style="border-bottom:1px solid Sienna; background-color:Wheat; padding:0.2em 0.5em 0.2em 0.5em; font-size:100%; font-weight:bold;">
Truesdell rate of the Cauchy stress
</div>
<div style="padding:2em 5em 0em 3em;"> 
<math display="block">
  \overset{\circ}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} = \dot{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} - \boldsymbol{l}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma} - \boldsymbol{\sigma} \cdot \boldsymbol{l}^T + \text{tr}(\boldsymbol{l})~\boldsymbol{\sigma}
</math>
where <math>\boldsymbol{l}</math> is the velocity gradient: <math>\boldsymbol{l} = \dot{\boldsymbol{F}} \cdot \boldsymbol{F}^{-1}</math>.

{{math proof | proof = We start with
<math display="block">
  \overset{\circ}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} = J^{-1}~\boldsymbol{F}\cdot
       \left[\cfrac{d}{dt}\left(J~\boldsymbol{F}^{-1}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\boldsymbol{F}^{-T}\right)\right]
       \cdot\boldsymbol{F}^T ~.
</math>
Expanding the derivative inside the square brackets, we get
<math display="block"> \begin{align}
  \overset{\circ}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} & = 
    J^{-1}~\boldsymbol{F}\cdot(\dot{J}~\boldsymbol{F}^{-1}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\boldsymbol{F}^{-T})\cdot\boldsymbol{F}^T + 
    J^{-1}~\boldsymbol{F}\cdot(J~\dot{\boldsymbol{F}^{-1}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\boldsymbol{F}^{-T})\cdot\boldsymbol{F}^T \\
    & + 
    J^{-1}~\boldsymbol{F}\cdot(J~\boldsymbol{F}^{-1}\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\cdot\boldsymbol{F}^{-T})\cdot\boldsymbol{F}^T + 
    J^{-1}~\boldsymbol{F}\cdot(J~\boldsymbol{F}^{-1}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol{F}^{-T}})\cdot\boldsymbol{F}^T 
\end{align} </math>
or,
<math display="block">
  \overset{\circ}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} = J^{-1}~\dot{J}~\boldsymbol{\sigma} + 
    \boldsymbol{F}\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol{F}^{-1}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma} + \dot{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} + 
    \boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol{F}^{-T}}\cdot\boldsymbol{F}^T 
</math>
Now,
<math display="block"> \boldsymbol{F}\cdot\boldsymbol{F}^{-1} = \boldsymbol{\mathit{1}}</math>
Therefore,
<math display="block">
  \frac{d}{dt}\left(\boldsymbol{F}\cdot\boldsymbol{F}^{-1}\right) = 0
  \quad \implies \quad
  \dot{\boldsymbol{F}}\cdot\boldsymbol{F}^{-1} + \boldsymbol{F}\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol{F}^{-1}} = 0
</math>
or,
<math display="block">
  \dot{\boldsymbol{F}^{-1}} = - \boldsymbol{F}^{-1}\cdot\boldsymbol{l} \quad \implies \quad
  \dot{\boldsymbol{F}^{-T}} = - \boldsymbol{l}^T\cdot\boldsymbol{F}^{-T}
</math>
where the velocity gradient <math>\boldsymbol{l} = \dot{\boldsymbol{F}}\cdot\boldsymbol{F}^{-1}</math>.

Also, the rate of change of volume is given by
<math display="block"> \dot{J} = J~\text{tr}(\boldsymbol{d}) = J~\text{tr}(\boldsymbol{l}) </math>
where <math>\boldsymbol{d}</math> is the rate of deformation tensor.

Therefore,
<math display="block">
  \overset{\circ}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} = J^{-1}~J~\text{tr}(\boldsymbol{l})~\boldsymbol{\sigma} - 
    \boldsymbol{F}\cdot\boldsymbol{F}^{-1}\cdot\boldsymbol{l}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma} + \dot{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} - 
    \boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\boldsymbol{l}^T\cdot\boldsymbol{F}^{-T}\cdot\boldsymbol{F}^T 
</math>
or,
<math display="block">
  \overset{\circ}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} = \dot{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} - \boldsymbol{l}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma} - \boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\boldsymbol{l}^T + \text{tr}(\boldsymbol{l})~\boldsymbol{\sigma}
</math>
}}</div>
|}
It can be shown that the Truesdell rate is objective.

== Truesdell rate of the Kirchhoff stress ==
The Truesdell rate of the Kirchhoff stress can be obtained by noting that
<math display="block"> \boldsymbol{S} = \phi^{*}[\boldsymbol{\tau}] ~;~~ \boldsymbol{\tau} = \phi_{*}[\boldsymbol{S}]</math>
and defining
<math display="block"> \overset{\circ}{\boldsymbol{\tau}} = \phi_{*}[\dot{\boldsymbol{S}}]</math>
Expanded out, this means that
<math display="block">
  \overset{\circ}{\boldsymbol{\tau}} = \boldsymbol{F}\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol{S}}\cdot\boldsymbol{F}^T
     = \boldsymbol{F}\cdot
       \left[\cfrac{d}{dt}\left(\boldsymbol{F}^{-1}\cdot\boldsymbol{\tau}\cdot\boldsymbol{F}^{-T}\right)\right]
       \cdot\boldsymbol{F}^T
     = \mathcal{L}_\varphi[\boldsymbol{\tau}]
</math>
Therefore, ''' the Lie derivative of <math>\boldsymbol{\tau}</math> is the same as the Truesdell rate of the Kirchhoff stress'''.

Following the same process as for the Cauchy stress above, we can show that
{| cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" style="margin:0em 0em 1em 0em; width:80%"
| colspan="2" style="width:80%; horizontal-align:right; vertical-align:top; border:1px solid Sienna; background-color:White;" |
<div style="border-bottom:1px solid Sienna; background-color:Wheat; padding:0.2em 0.5em 0.2em 0.5em; font-size:100%; font-weight:bold;">
Truesdell rate of the Kirchhoff stress
</div>
<div style="padding:2em 5em 0em 3em;"> 
<math display="block"> \overset{\circ}{\boldsymbol{\tau}} = \dot{\boldsymbol{\tau}} - \boldsymbol{l}\cdot\boldsymbol{\tau} - \boldsymbol{\tau}\cdot\boldsymbol{l}^T </math>
</div>
|}

== Green-Naghdi rate of the Cauchy stress ==
This is a special form of the Lie derivative (or the Truesdell rate of the Cauchy stress).  Recall that the Truesdell rate of the Cauchy stress is given by
<math display="block">
  \overset{\circ}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} = J^{-1}~\boldsymbol{F}\cdot
       \left[\cfrac{d}{dt}\left(J~\boldsymbol{F}^{-1}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\boldsymbol{F}^{-T}\right)\right]
       \cdot\boldsymbol{F}^T ~.
</math>
From the [[polar decomposition]] theorem we have
<math display="block"> \boldsymbol{F} = \boldsymbol{R}\cdot\boldsymbol{U}</math>
where <math>\boldsymbol{R}</math> is the orthogonal rotation tensor (<math>\boldsymbol{R}^{-1} = \boldsymbol{R}^T</math>)
and <math>\boldsymbol{U}</math> is the symmetric, positive definite, right stretch.

If we assume that <math>\boldsymbol{U} = \boldsymbol{\mathit{1}}</math> we get <math>\boldsymbol{F} = \boldsymbol{R}</math>.  Also since there is no
stretch <math>J = 1</math> and we have <math>\boldsymbol{\tau} = \boldsymbol{\sigma}</math>. Note that this doesn't mean 
that there is not stretch in the actual body - this simplification is just
for the purposes of defining an objective stress rate. Therefore,
<math display="block">
  \overset{\circ}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} = \boldsymbol{R}\cdot
       \left[\cfrac{d}{dt}\left(\boldsymbol{R}^{-1}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\boldsymbol{R}^{-T}\right)\right]
       \cdot\boldsymbol{R}^T 
    = \boldsymbol{R}\cdot\left[\cfrac{d}{dt}\left(\boldsymbol{R}^T\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\boldsymbol{R}\right)\right]
       \cdot\boldsymbol{R}^T 
</math>
We can show that this expression can be simplified to the
commonly used form of the ''' Green-Naghdi''' rate
{| cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" style="margin:0em 0em 1em 0em; width:80%"
| colspan="2" style="width:80%; horizontal-align:right; vertical-align:top; border:1px solid Sienna; background-color:White;" |
<div style="border-bottom:1px solid Sienna; background-color:Wheat; padding:0.2em 0.5em 0.2em 0.5em; font-size:100%; font-weight:bold;">
Green-Naghdi rate of the Cauchy stress
</div>
<div style="padding:2em 5em 0em 3em;"> 
<math display="block">
  \overset{\square}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} = \dot{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} + \boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\boldsymbol{\Omega}
    - \boldsymbol{\Omega}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma} 
</math>
where <math>\boldsymbol{\Omega} = \dot{\boldsymbol{R}}\cdot\boldsymbol{R}^T</math>.

{{math proof | proof = Expanding out the derivative
<math display="block">
  \overset{\circ}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} = \boldsymbol{R}\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol{R}^T}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\boldsymbol{R}\cdot\boldsymbol{R}^T +
     \boldsymbol{R}\cdot\boldsymbol{R}^T\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\cdot\boldsymbol{R}\cdot\boldsymbol{R}^T +
     \boldsymbol{R}\cdot\boldsymbol{R}^T\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol{R}}\cdot\boldsymbol{R}^T 
</math>
or,
<math display="block">
  \overset{\circ}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} = \boldsymbol{R}\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol{R}^T}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma} + 
     \dot{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} + \boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol{R}}\cdot\boldsymbol{R}^T 
</math>
Now,
<math display="block">
  \boldsymbol{R}\cdot\boldsymbol{R}^T = \boldsymbol{\mathit{1}} \quad \implies \quad
  \dot{\boldsymbol{R}}\cdot\boldsymbol{R}^T = - \boldsymbol{R}\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol{R}^T}
</math>
Therefore,
<math display="block">
  \overset{\circ}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} = \dot{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} + \boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol{R}}\cdot\boldsymbol{R}^T 
    - \dot{\boldsymbol{R}}\cdot\boldsymbol{R}^T\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma} 
</math>
If we define the angular velocity as
<math display="block"> \boldsymbol{\Omega} = \dot{\boldsymbol{R}}\cdot\boldsymbol{R}^T</math>
we get the commonly used form of the ''' Green–Naghdi''' rate
<math display="block">
  \overset{\square}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} = \dot{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} + \boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\boldsymbol{\Omega}
    - \boldsymbol{\Omega}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma} 
</math>
}}</div>
|}

The Green–Naghdi rate of the Kirchhoff stress also has the form since the stretch is not taken into consideration, i.e.,
<math display="block">
  \overset{\square}{\boldsymbol{\tau}} = \dot{\boldsymbol{\tau}} + \boldsymbol{\tau}\cdot\boldsymbol{\Omega}
    - \boldsymbol{\Omega}\cdot\boldsymbol{\tau} 
</math>

== Zaremba-Jaumann rate of the Cauchy stress ==
The Zaremba-Jaumann rate of the Cauchy stress is a further specialization of the
Lie derivative (Truesdell rate).  This rate has the form
{| cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" style="margin:0em 0em 1em 0em; width:80%"
| colspan="2" style="width:80%; horizontal-align:right; vertical-align:top; border:1px solid Sienna; background-color:White;" |
<div style="border-bottom:1px solid Sienna; background-color:Wheat; padding:0.2em 0.5em 0.2em 0.5em; font-size:100%; font-weight:bold;">
Zaremba-Jaumann rate of the Cauchy stress
</div>
<div style="padding:2em 5em 0em 3em;"> 
<math display="block"> \overset{\triangle}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} = \dot{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} + \boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\boldsymbol{w} - \boldsymbol{w}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma} </math>
where <math>\boldsymbol{w}</math> is the spin tensor.</div>
|}

The Zaremba-Jaumann rate is used widely in computations primarily for two reasons
#it is relatively easy to implement.
#it leads to symmetric tangent moduli.

Recall that the spin tensor <math>\boldsymbol{w}</math> (the skew part of the velocity gradient)
can be expressed as
<math display="block">
  \boldsymbol{w} = \dot{\boldsymbol{R}}\cdot\boldsymbol{R}^T + \frac{1}{2}~\boldsymbol{R}\cdot(\dot{\boldsymbol{U}}\cdot\boldsymbol{U}^{-1} - 
     \boldsymbol{U}^{-1}\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol{U}})\cdot\boldsymbol{R}^T
</math>
Thus for pure rigid body motion
<math display="block">
  \boldsymbol{w} = \dot{\boldsymbol{R}}\cdot\boldsymbol{R}^T = \boldsymbol{\Omega}
</math>
Alternatively, we can consider the case of ''' proportional loading''' when the principal directions of strain remain constant. An example of this situation is the axial loading of a cylindrical bar. In that situation, since
<math display="block">
  \boldsymbol{U} = \begin{bmatrix}
\lambda_{X}\\
 & \lambda_{Y}\\
 &  & \lambda_{Z}\end{bmatrix}
</math>
we have
<math display="block"> \dot{\boldsymbol{U}} = \begin{bmatrix}
\dot{\lambda}_{X}\\
 & \dot{\lambda}_{Y}\\
 &  & \dot{\lambda}_{Z}
\end{bmatrix}</math>
Also,
<math display="block"> \boldsymbol{U}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}
1/\lambda_{X}\\
 & 1/\lambda_{Y}\\
 &  & 1/\lambda_{Z}
\end{bmatrix}</math>
of the Cauchy stress.
Therefore,
<math display="block">
  \dot{\boldsymbol{U}}\cdot\boldsymbol{U}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}
\dot{\lambda}_{X}/\lambda_{X}\\
 & \dot{\lambda}_{Y}/\lambda_{Y}\\
 &  & \dot{\lambda}_{Z}/\lambda_{Z}
\end{bmatrix} = U^{-1}\dot{U}
</math>
This once again gives
<math display="block"> \boldsymbol{w} = \dot{\boldsymbol{R}}\cdot\boldsymbol{R}^T = \boldsymbol{\Omega}</math>
In general, if we approximate
<math display="block"> \boldsymbol{w} \approx \dot{\boldsymbol{R}}\cdot\boldsymbol{R}^T </math>
the Green–Naghdi rate becomes the Zaremba-Jaumann rate of the Cauchy stress
<math display="block">
  \overset{\triangle}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} = \dot{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} + \boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\boldsymbol{w}
    - \boldsymbol{w}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma} 
</math>

== Other objective stress rates ==
There can be an infinite variety of objective stress rates. One of these
is the ''' Oldroyd stress rate'''
<math display="block">
  \overset{\triangledown}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} = \mathcal{L}_\varphi[\boldsymbol{\sigma}]
       = \boldsymbol{F}\cdot\left[\cfrac{d}{dt}\left(\boldsymbol{F}^{-1}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\boldsymbol{F}^{-T}\right)
          \right]\cdot\boldsymbol{F}^T
</math>
In simpler form, the Oldroyd rate is given by
<math display="block"> \overset{\triangledown}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} = \dot{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} - \boldsymbol{l}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma} - \boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\boldsymbol{l}^T </math>

If the current configuration is assumed to be the reference configuration then the pull back and push forward operations can be conducted using <math>\boldsymbol{F}^T</math> and <math>\boldsymbol{F}^{-T}</math> respectively.  The Lie derivative of the Cauchy stress is then called the ''' convective stress rate'''
<math display="block">
  \overset{\diamond}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} 
     = \boldsymbol{F}^{-T}\cdot\left[\cfrac{d}{dt}\left(\boldsymbol{F}^T\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\boldsymbol{F}\right)
          \right]\cdot\boldsymbol{F}^{-1}
</math>
In simpler form, the convective rate is given by
<math display="block"> \overset{\diamond}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} = \dot{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} + \boldsymbol{l}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma} + \boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\boldsymbol{l}^T </math>

== Objective stress rates in finite strain inelasticity ==
Many materials undergo inelastic deformations caused by plasticity and damage. These material behaviors cannot be described in terms of a potential. It is also often the case that no memory of the initial virgin state exists, particularly when large deformations are involved.{{CN|date=February 2025}} The constitutive relation is typically defined in incremental form in such cases to make the computation of stresses and deformations easier.{{CN|date=February 2025}}

=== The incremental loading procedure ===
For a small enough load step, the material deformation can be characterized by the [[infinitesimal strain theory|small (or linearized) strain increment tensor]]{{CN|date=February 2025}} 
<math display="block">
   \boldsymbol{e} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left[\boldsymbol{\nabla}\mathbf{u} + (\boldsymbol{\nabla}\mathbf{u})^T\right]
   \quad \equiv \quad e_{ij} = \tfrac{1}{2}(u_{i,j} + u_{j,i})
 </math> 
where <math>\mathbf{u}</math> is the displacement increment of the continuum points. The time derivative 
<math display="block">
 \frac{\partial\boldsymbol{e}}{\partial t} = \dot{\boldsymbol{e}} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left[\boldsymbol{\nabla}\mathbf{v} + (\boldsymbol{\nabla}\mathbf{v})^T\right]
   \quad \equiv \quad\dot{e}_{ij} = \tfrac{1}{2} (v_{i,j} + v_{j,i})
 </math> 
is the [[strain rate tensor]] (also called the velocity strain) and <math>\mathbf{v} = \dot{\mathbf{u}}</math> is the material point velocity or displacement rate. For finite strains, measures from the [[Finite strain theory#Seth–Hill family of generalized strain tensors|Seth–Hill family]] (also called Doyle–Ericksen tensors) can be used:
<math display="block"> \mathbf E_{(m)}=\frac{1}{2m}(\mathbf U^{2m}- \mathbf I) </math>
where <math>\mathbf{U}</math> is the right stretch. A second-order approximation of these tensors is
<math display="block"> \mathbf{E}_{(m)} \approx \boldsymbol{e} + {\tfrac 1 2}(\nabla\mathbf{u})^T\cdot\nabla\mathbf{u} - (1 - m) \boldsymbol{e} \cdot \boldsymbol{e}</math>

=== Energy-consistent objective stress rates ===
Consider a material element of unit initial volume, starting from an initial state under initial Cauchy (or true) stress <math>\boldsymbol{\sigma}_0</math> and let <math>\boldsymbol{\sigma}</math> be the Cauchy stress in the final configuration. Let <math>W</math> be the work done (per unit initial volume) by the internal forces during an incremental deformation from this initial state. Then the variation <math>\delta W</math> corresponds to the variation in the work done due to a variation in the displacement <math>\delta \mathbf{u}</math>.  The displacement variation has to satisfy the displacement boundary conditions.

Let <math>\boldsymbol{S}_{(m)}</math> be an objective stress tensor in the initial configuration. Define the stress increment with respect to the initial configuration as <math>\boldsymbol{S} = \boldsymbol{S}_{(m)} - \boldsymbol{\sigma}_0</math>. Alternatively, if <math>\boldsymbol{P}</math> is the unsymmetric first Piola–Kirchhoff stress referred to the initial configuration, the increment in stress can be expressed as <math>\boldsymbol{T} = \boldsymbol{P} - \boldsymbol{\sigma}_0</math>.

==== Variation of work done ====
Then the variation in work done can be expressed as
<math display="block">
   \delta W = \boldsymbol{S}_{(m)}:\delta\boldsymbol{E}_{(m)} = \boldsymbol{P}:\delta\nabla\mathbf{u}
 </math>
where the finite strain measure <math>\boldsymbol{E}_{(m)}</math> is energy conjugate to the stress measure <math>\boldsymbol{\sigma}^{(m)}</math>.  Expanded out, 
<math display="block">
   \delta W = \left(\boldsymbol{S}+\boldsymbol{\sigma}_0\right):\delta\boldsymbol{E}_{(m)} 
            = \left(\boldsymbol{T}+\boldsymbol{\sigma}_0\right):\delta\nabla\mathbf{u} \,.
 </math>
The objectivity of stress tensor <math>\boldsymbol{S}_{(m)}</math> is ensured by its transformation as a second-order tensor under coordinate rotations (which causes the principal stresses to be independent from coordinate rotations) and by the correctness of <math>\boldsymbol{S}_{(m)}:\delta\boldsymbol{E}_{(m)}</math> as a second-order energy expression.

From the symmetry of the Cauchy stress, we have 
<math display="block">
  \boldsymbol{\sigma}_0:\delta\nabla\mathbf{u} = \boldsymbol{\sigma}_0:\delta\boldsymbol{e} \,.
</math>
For small variations in strain, using the approximation
<math display="block">
  \boldsymbol{S}:\delta\boldsymbol{E}_{(m)}  \approx  \boldsymbol{S}:\delta\nabla\mathbf{u}
 </math>
and the expansions
<math display="block">
   \boldsymbol{\sigma}_0:\delta\boldsymbol{E}_{(m)}  = \boldsymbol{\sigma}_0:\left[\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{E}_{(m)}}{\partial \nabla\mathbf{u}}:\delta\nabla\mathbf{u}\right] ~,~~
   \boldsymbol{\sigma}_0:\delta\boldsymbol{e}  = \boldsymbol{\sigma}_0:\left[\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{e}}{\partial \nabla\mathbf{u}}:\delta\nabla\mathbf{u}\right]  
 </math>
we get the equation
<math display="block">
  \boldsymbol{\sigma}_0:\left[\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{E}_{(m)}}{\partial \nabla\mathbf{u}}:\delta\nabla\mathbf{u}\right] + \boldsymbol{S}:\delta\nabla\mathbf{u} = \boldsymbol{\sigma}_0:\left[\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{e}}{\partial \nabla\mathbf{u}}:\delta\nabla\mathbf{u}\right] + \boldsymbol{T}:\delta\nabla\mathbf{u} \,.
 </math>
Imposing the variational condition that the resulting equation must be valid for any strain gradient <math>\delta\nabla\mathbf{u}</math>, we have<ref name="Baz71" />
{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> \boldsymbol{S} = \boldsymbol{T} - \boldsymbol{\sigma}_0:\left[\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{E}_{(m)}}{\partial \nabla\mathbf{u}}-\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{e}}{\partial \nabla\mathbf{u}}\right] </math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}}
We can also write the above equation as
{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> \boldsymbol{S}_{(m)} = \boldsymbol{P} - \boldsymbol{\sigma}_0:\frac{\partial}{\partial \nabla\mathbf{u}}\left[\boldsymbol{E}_{(m)} - \boldsymbol{e}\right] \,.  </math>|{{EquationRef|2}}}}

==== Time derivatives ====
The Cauchy stress and the first Piola-Kirchhoff stress are related by (see [[Stress measures]])
<math display="block"> \boldsymbol{\sigma} = \boldsymbol{P}\cdot\boldsymbol{F}^T J^{-1} = (\boldsymbol{P} + \boldsymbol{P}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{u}^T) J^{-1} \,. </math>
For small incremental deformations, 
<math display="block"> J^{-1} \approx 1 - \nabla\cdot\mathbf{u} \,. </math>
Therefore,
<math display="block">
   \Delta\boldsymbol{\sigma} = \boldsymbol{\sigma} - \boldsymbol{\sigma}_0
     \approx  (\boldsymbol{P} + \boldsymbol{P}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{u}^T) (1 - \nabla\cdot\mathbf{u}) - \boldsymbol{\sigma}_0 \,.
 </math>
Substituting <math>\boldsymbol{T} + \boldsymbol{\sigma}_0 = \boldsymbol{P}</math>,
<math display="block">
   \Delta\boldsymbol{\sigma} \approx [\boldsymbol{T} + \boldsymbol{\sigma}_0 + (\boldsymbol{T} + \boldsymbol{\sigma}_0)\cdot\nabla\mathbf{u}^T] (1 - \nabla\cdot\mathbf{u}) - \boldsymbol{\sigma}_0 \,.
 </math>
For small increments of stress <math>\boldsymbol{T}</math> relative to the initial stress <math>\boldsymbol{\sigma}_0</math>, the above reduces to
{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> \Delta\boldsymbol{\sigma} \approx \boldsymbol{T} - \boldsymbol{\sigma}_0 (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}) + \boldsymbol{\sigma}_0 \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u}^T \,. </math>|{{EquationRef|3}}}}
From equations (1) and (3) we have
{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> \boldsymbol{S} = \Delta\boldsymbol{\sigma} + \boldsymbol{\sigma}_0 (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}) - \boldsymbol{\sigma}_0 \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u}^T- \boldsymbol{\sigma}_0:\left[\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{E}_{(m)}}{\partial \nabla\mathbf{u}}-\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{e}}{\partial \nabla\mathbf{u}}\right] </math>|{{EquationRef|4}}}}
Recall that <math>\boldsymbol{S}</math> is an increment of the stress tensor measure <math>\boldsymbol{S}_{(m)}</math>.
Defining the stress rate
<math display="block"> \boldsymbol{S} =: \overset{\circ}{\boldsymbol{S}}_{(m)} \Delta t </math>
and noting that
<math display="block"> \Delta\boldsymbol{\sigma} = \dot{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} \Delta t </math>
we can write equation (4) as
{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> \overset{\circ}{\boldsymbol{S}}_{(m)} \Delta t = \dot{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} \Delta t + \boldsymbol{\sigma}_0 (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}) \Delta t - \boldsymbol{\sigma}_0 \cdot \nabla \mathbf{v}^T \Delta t - \boldsymbol{\sigma}_0:\left[\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{E}_{(m)}}{\partial \nabla\mathbf{u}}-\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{e}}{\partial \nabla\mathbf{u}}\right]</math>|{{EquationRef|5}}}}
Taking the limit at <math>\Delta t \rightarrow 0</math>, and noting that <math>\boldsymbol{\sigma}_0 = \boldsymbol{\sigma}</math> at this limit, one gets the following expression for the objective stress rate associated with the strain measure <math>\boldsymbol{E}_{(m)}</math>:
{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> \overset{\circ}{\boldsymbol{S}}_{(m)} = \dot{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} + \boldsymbol{\sigma}(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v})  - \boldsymbol{\sigma} \cdot \nabla \mathbf{v}^T - \boldsymbol{\sigma} : \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \left[\frac{\partial}{\partial \nabla\mathbf{u}}\left(\boldsymbol{E}_{(m)} - \boldsymbol{e}\right)\right] \,. </math>|{{EquationRef|6}}}}
Here <math>\dot \sigma_{ij} = \partial \sigma_{ij} /\partial t</math> = material rate of Cauchy stress (i.e., the rate in Lagrangian coordinates of the initial stressed state).

==== Work-conjugate stress rates ====
A rate for which there exists no legitimate finite strain tensor <math>\boldsymbol{E}_{(m)}</math> associated according to Eq. (6) is energetically inconsistent, i.e., its use violates energy balance (i.e., the [[first law of thermodynamics]]).

Evaluating Eq. (6) for general <math>m</math> and for <math>m=2</math>, one gets a general expression for the objective stress rate:<ref name="Baz71" /><ref name="BazCed91" />
{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> \overset{\circ}{\boldsymbol{S}}_{(m)} = \overset{\circ}{\boldsymbol{S}}_{(2)} + \tfrac{1}{2}(2 - m) [\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot \dot \boldsymbol{e} + (\boldsymbol{\sigma} \cdot \dot \boldsymbol{e})^T]  </math>|{{EquationRef|7}}}}
where <math>\overset{\circ}{\boldsymbol{S}}_{(2)}</math> is the objective stress rate associated with the Green-Lagrangian strain (<math>m=2</math>).

In particular,
* <math>m=2</math> gives the '''Truesdell stress rate'''
* <math>m=0</math> gives the '''Zaremba-Jaumann rate of Kirchhoff stress'''
* <math>m=1</math> gives the '''Biot stress rate'''

(Note that m = 2 leads to [[Engesser's formula]] for critical load in shear buckling, while m = -2 leads to [[Haringx's formula]] which can give critical loads differing by >100%).

==== Non work-conjugate stress rates ====
Other rates, used in most commercial codes, which are not work-conjugate to any finite strain tensor are:<ref name="BazCed91" />
* the '''Zaremba-Jaumann, or corotational, rate of Cauchy stress''': It differs from Zaremba-Jaumann rate of Kirchhoff stress by missing the rate of relative volume change of material. The lack of work-conjugacy is usually not a serious problem since that term is negligibly small for many materials and zero for incompressible materials (but in indentation of a sandwich plate with foam core, this rate can give an error of >30% in the indentation force).
* the '''Cotter–Rivlin rate''' corresponds to <math>m = -2</math> but it again misses the volumetric term.
* the '''Green–Naghdi rate''': This objective stress rate is not work-conjugate to any finite strain tensor, not only because of the missing volumetric term but also because the material rotation velocity is not exactly equal to the [[spin tensor]]. In the vast majority of applications, the errors in the energy calculation, caused by these differences, are negligible. However, it must be pointed out that a large energy error was already demonstrated for a case with shear strains and rotations exceeding about 0.25.<ref name="BazVor13"/>
* the '''Oldroyd rate'''.

==== Objective rates and Lie derivatives ====
The objective stress rates could also be regarded as the Lie derivatives of various types of stress tensor (i.e., the associated covariant, contravariant and mixed components of Cauchy stress) and their linear combinations.<ref name="MarHug83" /> The Lie derivative does not include the concept of work-conjugacy.

== Tangential stiffness moduli and their transformations to achieve energy consistency ==
The tangential stress-strain relation has generally the form
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\dot S_{ij}^{(m)} = C_{ijkl}^{(m)} \dot e_{kl}</math>|{{EquationRef|6}}}}
where <math>C_{ijkl}^{(m)}</math> are the tangential moduli (components of a 4th-order tensor) associated with strain tensor <math>\epsilon_{ij}^{(m)}</math>. They are different for different choices of <math>m</math>, and are related as follows:
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\left[C_{ijkl}^{(m)} - C^{(2)}_{ijkl} - {\tfrac 1 4}(2-m)(S_{ik}\delta_{jl} + S_{jk}\delta_{il} + S_{il}\delta_{jk} + S_{jl}\delta_{ik}) \right] v_{k,l}= 0</math>|{{EquationRef|7}}}}
From the fact that Eq. (7) must hold true for any velocity gradient <math>v_{k,l}</math>, it follows that:<ref name="Baz71" />
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">C_{ijkl}^{(m)} = C^{(2)}_{ijkl} + (2-m)[S_{ik}\delta_{jl}]_\mathrm{sym},~~[S_{ik}\delta_{jl}]_\mathrm{sym} = {\tfrac 1 4} (S_{ik}\delta_{jl} + S_{jk}\delta_{il} + S_{il}\delta_{jk} + S_{jl}\delta_{ik})</math>|{{EquationRef|8}}}}
where <math>C_{ijkl}^{(2)}</math> are the tangential moduli associated with the Green–Lagrangian strain (<math>m=2</math>), taken as a reference, <math>S_{ij}</math> = current Cauchy stress, and <math>\delta_{ij}</math> = [[Kronecker delta]] (or unit tensor).

Eq. (8) can be used to convert one objective stress rate to another. Since <math>S_{ij} \dot e_{kk} = (S_{ij} \delta_{kl}) \delta e_{kl}</math>, the transformation<ref name="Baz71" /><ref name="BazCed91" />
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">C_{ijkl}^{\mathrm{conj}} = C_{ijkl}^{\mathrm{nonconj}} + S_{ij}\delta_{kl}</math>|{{EquationRef|9}}}}
can further correct for the absence of the term <math>S_{ij} v_{k,k}</math> (note that the term <math>S_{ij}\delta_{km}</math> does not allow interchanging subscripts <math>ij</math> with <math>kl</math>, which means that its absence breaks the major symmetry of the tangential moduli tensor <math>C_{ijkl}^{\mathrm{nonconj}}</math>).

Large strain often develops when the material behavior becomes nonlinear, due to plasticity or damage. Then the primary cause of stress dependence of the tangential moduli is the physical behavior of material. What Eq. (8) means that the nonlinear dependence of <math>C_{ijkl}</math> on the stress must be different for different objective stress rates. Yet none of them is fundamentally preferable, except if there exists one stress rate, one <math>m</math>, for which the moduli can be considered constant.
